messages.content:
You are verifying one structured PFAS study evidence record against the
complete source evidence cited by that record.

You receive:
1. the review task and task-specific extraction objective;
2. the held-out anchor identifiers;
3. one extracted evidence record; and
4. the complete source chunks or inspected source-page text referenced by the
   record.

Judge only source support and transcription. Do not reward usefulness,
verbosity, or agreement with general background knowledge.

Assess every substantive populated source-dependent field against only its
attached field-level locators. Do not create separate assessments for locator
arrays, record IDs, or formatting metadata:
- supported: the cited evidence directly supports the field and its material
  qualifiers;
- partially_supported: the core statement is supported but a material
  qualifier, condition, denominator, or scope is missing;
- unsupported: the cited evidence does not establish the field;
- contradicted: the cited evidence directly conflicts with the field.

For quantitative_findings, value must contain an actual number, censored or
approximate number, range, or explicit ND/not-detected result. A unit-shaped
string such as "nmol/L" in value with an empty unit is a unit error even when
the source mentions that concentration scale. Do not silently reinterpret one
schema field as another. Confirm that value matches value_form; explanatory
text and uncertainty belong in qualifiers.

Classify endpoint_type from the measured basis, not the source's terminology.
Parent-compound loss alone is not destruction; phase transfer is not
degradation; inorganic fluoride release or fluorine-balance closure establishes
defluorination but not mineralization. Mineralization requires direct
carbon-fate evidence such as measured CO2/inorganic carbon or a carbon balance.
If an author calls defluorination mineralization without that evidence, retain
the author phrase only as reported_term and mark endpoint_type=mineralization
unsupported with error_type=endpoint_classification.

Comparability is an analyst-derived judgment. Do not require the source to
state the comparability conclusion verbatim. Instead, judge whether its status
and reason follow conservatively from supported cited fields for matrix, PFAS
scope, scale, conditions, endpoint, unit, and denominator.

An author_reported limitation requires direct source support. A
design_inferred limitation is supported when it follows necessarily from
cited design facts; absence from the supplied packet is not a study
limitation.

Classify errors as numeric_transcription, unit, qualifier,
endpoint_classification, source_attribution, other, or none. A record is usable
only if its source identity, matrix, treatment, endpoints, and quantitative
findings are not unsupported or contradicted in a way that would mislead
  synthesis. A usable record can still contain non-core fields that synthesis
must exclude according to their field assessments.

For metric consistency, always emit separate assessments with these exact
field-path forms when the corresponding item exists:
- `quantitative_findings[i].value`;
- `quantitative_findings[i].unit`;
- `operating_conditions[i].value`;
- `operating_conditions[i].unit`;
- `endpoints[i].endpoint_type`; and
- `comparability.status`.

Other substantive fields may be assessed individually or as a whole object,
but do not omit these required assessment types and do not emit a required
field path more than once.

Report anchor_exclusion_violation=true if the source resolves to any held-out
anchor DOI, URL, exact title, or corpus source.

Return one JSON object that follows the supplied verification schema exactly.

field_assessments.reason: The record DOI/URL exactly matches the source DOI and URL: 10.1016/j.chemosphere.2022.137004 / https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chemosphere.2022.137004.

The cited text shows the study reports mass-balance recoveries for PFASs, TOC, and terminal PFAAs (70–130% ranges, TOC 111.3%) but does not provide detailed PFAS-specific removal/enrichment for the AFFF groundwater at these conditions; inferring that the record is mainly descriptive for mass-balance and co-surfactant effects is reasonable.

E02 and E04 document quantitative recoveries and TOC distribution (including HPMC) and mass-balance closure, but not detailed PFAS removal/enrichment metrics for the AFFF groundwater. Describing the study as mainly qualitative/comparative for co-surfactant effects and mass balance follows from these data.

E02 and E04 state that HPMC contributed 93.9% of TOC initially and that TOC from HPMC in foam accounted for 87.2% of total TOC, with the authors noting near complete removal of HPMC from the treated bottom solution. Classifying this as a removal endpoint is consistent with the text.

E02 and E04 indicate that most HPMC was removed from the bottom solution and that 87.2% of TOC in foam was from HPMC, and explicitly mention near-complete removal of HPMC. The interpretation that HPMC strongly partitions to foam and is nearly completely removed from the treated bottom solution is accurate.

E02 and E04 report recoveries (70–130%) and explicitly refer to mass balance of target PFASs, TOC, and terminal PFAAs. Treating this as an “other” endpoint focused on mass balance is consistent with the measurement basis.

E02 notes overall PFAS recoveries within 70–130% (except PFDA) and TOC recovery of 111.3%; E04 reports terminal PFAA recoveries within 70–130% and that mass balance was deemed satisfactory. The interpretation correctly summarizes these statements.

The endpoint describes PFAS fraction of TOC and HPMC’s contribution to TOC. This is not a conventional removal/destruction endpoint but a composition/partitioning measure, so classifying as “other” is appropriate.

E02 states PFASs accounted for <0.05% of TOC, while HPMC contributed 93.9% of TOC in the pre-treated solution and that most HPMC TOC moved to foam. The interpretation accurately reflects this TOC composition and distribution information.

E07 confirms AFFF-contaminated groundwater among the environmental samples; E02–E04 show detailed mass-balance evaluation only for this matrix with added HPMC. Concluding that results may not generalize to other waters or to cases without thickener is a reasonable design-inferred limitation.

Within the cited text for AFFF groundwater, only overall recoveries and TOC/HPMC distributions are reported; specific PFAS removal percentages and enrichment factors for this matrix are not. Stating that this limits quantitative assessment of FF efficiency for individual PFAS is a valid design-inferred limitation.

E07 shows multi-stage FF experiments on environmental samples including an AFFF-contaminated groundwater; E02–E04 show that the AFFF groundwater was treated and that HPMC was used in an additional single-stage experiment. Describing the matrix as AFFF-contaminated groundwater with PFAS mixtures and organic carbon and noting HPMC addition in some experiments is consistent with the text.

E07 describes multi-stage FF treatment of environmental samples; E02 mentions an additional single-stage experiment under the same conditions. Thus, stating that both single-stage and multi-stage FF were used is supported.
The field correctly has a null unit for a categorical description of operating mode, which is appropriate given the qualitative nature of the parameter.

E02 explicitly mentions the effect of adding HPMC in the additional single-stage experiment; E04 discusses HPMC’s removal and its use as an additive in FF treatment. Identifying hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (HPMC) as an added component is supported.
No numerical quantity is reported for this categorical operating condition, so a null unit is appropriate.

The cited text confirms that HPMC was added and removed efficiently, but within these locators it does not explicitly label HPMC as a “thickener” or state that it was added specifically to facilitate foaming, even though that is likely described elsewhere in the paper.

E02 and E04 refer to TOC recovery and TOC from HPMC in original, treated bottom, and foam solutions; E08 notes that TOC analysis was performed. Describing TOC analysis of original, bottom, and foam solutions is accurate.
This is a procedural/analytical condition, not a numeric parameter; leaving the unit null is appropriate.

E04 clearly states that TOP assay results were obtained for terminal PFAAs in the original sample, treated bottom solution, and foam solution after oxidative treatment. The description of terminal PFAA concentrations measured before and after oxidation is supported.
TOP assay use is qualitative here; no numeric value is provided, so a null unit is appropriate.

E07 confirms FF experiments with environmental samples including AFFF-contaminated groundwater containing PFASs. The text here acknowledges a PFAS mixture without specifying individual compounds, matching the available information.
E04 lists PFBA, PFPeA, PFHxA, PFHpA, PFOA, PFUdA, and PFOS as PFAAs whose concentrations increased after TOP assay, and refers to them as terminal PFAAs. The described PFCA/PFSA list is accurate.
E02 states: “The overall recovery for each of the PFASs after the multi-stage FF treatment was within 70–130%, except for PFDA (Fig. S11).” The recorded range 70–130 matches this statement.
Recovery is explicitly expressed in percent in E02, so the unit “%” is correct.
E02 reports: “The average TOC recovery was 111.3% (Fig. S9).” The recorded value 111.3 matches exactly.
The TOC recovery is explicitly given as a percentage in E02, so “%” is correct.
E02 states: “PFASs accounted for <0.05% of TOC in samples (Table S6) …”. The value “<0.05” with inequality form correctly reflects this.
The PFAS share of TOC is explicitly expressed as a percent of TOC, so unit “%” is appropriate.
E02 reports: “HPMC contributed 93.9% of the TOC in the pre-treated original solution (Fig. S12).” The recorded value 93.9 matches exactly.
The contribution of HPMC is expressed as a percent of TOC, so the unit “%” is correct.
E04 states: “the TOC from HPMC in the collected foam accounted for 87.2% of total TOC (Fig. S12).” The recorded value 87.2 matches exactly.
The HPMC-derived TOC fraction is given as a percent of total TOC, so unit “%” is correct.
E04 states: “The recovery of each terminal PFAA was within 70%–130% (Fig. S13d).” The recorded range 70–130 matches this statement.
Terminal PFAA recovery is expressed in percent, so the unit “%” is appropriate.

E04 notes that after the oxidative TOP assay, concentrations of PFBA, PFPeA, PFHxA, PFHpA, PFOA, PFUdA and PFOS increased, and links this to presence of PFAA precursors in AFFF formulations and AFFF-impacted samples, matching the statement.

E03 describes a small acrylic column FF setup (bench-type apparatus), and E07 notes experiments with environmental samples including AFFF-contaminated groundwater. E02–E04 describe single- and multi-stage operations and HPMC use. Together these support the description of a bench-scale FF system applied to environmental water with and without thickener, in single- and multi-stage modes.

E07 describes multi-stage FF of AFFF-contaminated groundwater under conditions in Table S2. E02 mentions an additional single-stage experiment under the same conditions to explore mass balance and the effect of adding HPMC. E03 provides that all use the same FF column apparatus. The treatment description accurately summarises these elements.

result.record_usable_rationale: Core elements—source identity, matrix (AFFF-contaminated groundwater), foam-fractionation treatment configuration, co-addition of HPMC, and all quantitative mass-balance and TOC distribution results—are directly supported by the cited text. Only a minor qualifier (explicitly calling HPMC a “thickener” to facilitate foaming) is partially supported, which does not affect use of the record for synthesis on operating-condition effects and mass balance.
